Course Objectives
This course leads the students to understand the need of programming in various disciplines, basic concepts of algorithm, the process of computational problem solving in an efficient manner, how to write simple programs using C, pointers, dynamic memory allocation, arrays, functions, recursions, file handling and error handling, and basic concepts of modularity.

text:
Course Outcomes
At the end of the course students will be able to:

Implement a given algorithm in C by using standard programming constructs such as pointers, arrays, repetitions, functions, modules, aggregated data (arrays, lists, etc.).
Explain the output of a given C program, and identify and correct errors in a given C program (debug).
Write simple programs to solve math problems using the C programming language.

title: W01: Introduction
text:
PAGAL Notes
PAGAL — Perspectives on Algorithms, Generative AI & Learning: the week’s informal column.

📽️ In slides: PAGAL — Programming in the Age of AI — this week’s column as a presentation: the paradigm shift, the Specify–Verify loop, architects over bricklayers, and Computational X. The long-reads follow below.

On telescopes — and on checking your quotes.
This week’s deck leans on a famous line: “Computer science is not about machines, in the same way that astronomy is not about telescopes.” The internet will tell you, with great confidence, that Edsger Dijkstra said it (so will framed posters, and so will several AI assistants). We checked. The trail — documented at Quote Investigator — leads elsewhere: Alan Perlis was making the telescope comparison as early as 1968; the closest early match in print is science writer George Johnson in 1986; and the polished modern form belongs to mathematician Michael Fellows, writing with Ian Parberry in the early 1990s. Dijkstra would very likely have agreed — but there is no verified record of him saying it.
Why open a programming course’s first column with quote forensics? Because this is the whole course in miniature: a claim can be plausible, widely repeated, and wrong — and the only defense is to check it against a source. You will spend the semester doing precisely that with programs. Not “does this code look right?” but “does it meet what was asked?” Not “the AI said so” but “show me the witness.” The habit transfers both ways.
And the line itself? It survives the correction. Whoever said it, you proved it this week without noticing: you programmed a turtle — no silicon in sight — and everything that mattered was the plan. The machine is the telescope. Computing is the astronomy.

Programming in the age of AI — or, what exactly is our job now?
Here is the dilemma, stated without cushioning. For seventy years, the deal was: humans think, computers execute. That deal has been renegotiated while nobody asked us. Today the computer can write the program. It can run the program — that part was always true. And it can even make a show of verifying the program. Writer, runner, checker — all in the machine. So what, precisely, are you here to learn for four months?
Start with the economics, because they are brutal and clarifying. The software industry paid programmers well for one reason: creating software was scarce. Few people could do it, and the world wanted more of it than they could make. That scarcity is ending in front of us. A shopkeeper with no training can now describe an app and ship it. Non-tech people write working code every day. When a machine does something faster than you and often better, that something is a commodity — and nobody builds a career on a commodity. Typing programs is going the way of typing letters: everyone can, so it distinguishes no one.
But look carefully at what the machine actually took over. It took the middle of the loop — the Express step, plan-to-code. It did not take the two ends. Someone must still decide what should exist and state it so precisely that no ambiguity survives: that is Specify. And someone must still judge whether what came back is right — right for the stated problem, right at the edges, right when it fails: that is Verify. Be suspicious of the claim that the machine verifies itself; a checker that checks against a specification you never stated precisely is a dog grading its own homework. The verification is only ever as good as the specification, and both ends of the loop belong to whoever is willing to think. The Specify–Verify loop is the job now. The middle became free; the ends became everything.
This changes what kind of person you must become. Less a bricklayer, more an architect: someone who thinks in systems — how parts connect, where they can fail, what each piece promises the others. And it makes one unglamorous skill suddenly precious: reading. Comprehending code you did not write — in large quantities, quickly, skeptically — because from now on, most of the code in your life will arrive written by something else. You cannot audit what you cannot read, and you cannot read deeply what you do not understand down to the machine (which is why we will not skip the pointers, the memory, the compiler — the “obsolete” parts are the audit toolkit).
The one rule that compresses all of this: do not outsource the thinking. Outsource the typing — gladly. But the moment the problem statement, the plan, and the judgment of correctness come from the machine too, you are not using the tool; you are decoration around it. Everything in this course — the spec cards, the given/ensures habit, predict-before-run, “show me a witness” — is training for the two ends of the loop that remain, stubbornly, human.
And that points at the deepest change of all, which is not a skill but a temperament. When answers are cheap, the scarce thing is the person who still asks — curiosity, and the willingness to challenge yourself when the machine has made comfort so easy. It has never been simpler to appear competent without understanding anything: accept the generated code, ship it, move on. Which is exactly why the one who peeks under the hood, who asks “but why does this work?”, who deliberately attempts the problem the hard way once before accepting the easy way, pulls ahead — and keeps pulling ahead, because curiosity compounds and comfort doesn’t. The machine will happily do your thinking; it will never do your wondering.
That is how you prepare: not by racing the machine at the thing it commoditized, but by staying curious enough to keep asking what should exist, rigorous enough to judge what comes back — so good at specifying and verifying that the machine becomes your commodity.
A coda: whose problem is it, anyway?
One more turn of the screw before we close the week. We drew the chain as problem → plan → notation → executor — but problems don’t float free. They belong to someone, somewhere: a farmer pricing crops, a lab measuring an alloy, a clerk closing accounts. So the chain really starts one box earlier: world → problem → plan → notation → executor. A program is a claim about a world — “this is what mattered, and this is what should happen.” Get the world wrong, and everything downstream is flawlessly, efficiently wrong.
That gives Verify a twin, and the pair is worth memorizing now: “Did we build the thing right?” — does the program meet the spec; tests can answer this, and increasingly, so can machines. And “Did we build the right thing?” — does the spec serve the world it came from; only someone who knows that world, and cares about the person in it, can answer. The machine is getting very good at the first question. The second is not even in its vocabulary — it has never met your user.
This is why we keep insisting you know your own discipline deeply, and why a specification is never mere paperwork: it is a compressed model of someone else’s world, and writing one well takes the most unexpectedly technical of skills — asking, listening, and caring whose problem it is. Even the turtle taught this, quietly: the reward never came from running the program. It came from the drawing matching an intention — and intentions are things worlds have, not machines.

title: W02: The Computer, Revisited · Number Systems
text:
In Class
Monday — the computer, revisited (and programmed):

📽️ Deck 04 — The Computer, Revisited — the recap that closes Week 1’s loop: what the Turtle taught (programming) and what the Display machine taught (the stored procedure), the design’s proper name — von Neumann architecture — and the discussion trap: the Toy Computer adds and subtracts… so isn’t it just a calculator? (The dividing line is where the procedure lives.)
🧮 The Toy Computer — a complete von Neumann machine you can see all of at once: 40 cells (instructions tinted blue, data green — the machine can’t tell), ACC and PC on display, ten instructions, and a diary narrating every fetch–decode–execute. Work the six-rung ladder: one problem (adding two integers), one new idea per rung, ending at the recursion wall.
🔧 Under the Hood (a guided climb, in three parts: The Parts · Memory & Time · The Machine) — and what is the Toy Computer made of? Build every floor yourself: a switch flipped by a wire → gates → an adder → a flip-flop (from two NOR gates and a loop) → the clock → a complete flip-flop machine with a timing diagram. One precision to savour: Part 3’s machine is honestly built from flip-flops but its plan is frozen in its wiring — by Monday’s own dividing line, it is a calculator. The Toy Computer is the one with the stored program. The pair of them, side by side, are the lesson.

Tuesday — number systems:

📽️ Deck 03 — Number Systems — the week’s slides:

Radix-q positional systems — one idea behind every numeral (value = digits × powers of q); tally marks (q=1) to ternary to the popular costumes: decimal (q=10, courtesy of anatomy) and hexadecimal (q=16, binary’s shorthand). Binary (q=2) is what computers wear — because switches have two reliable states.
Conversions, both directions: binary→decimal by weights, decimal→binary by repeated division; hex ↔︎ binary four bits at a time.
Negative integers — there is no minus sign in a cell: sign-magnitude, one’s complement, and the winner, two’s complement (one adder does everything).
Real numbers — fixed point (the stuck ruler) and floating point (binary scientific notation), ending at the world standard: IEEE FP32 — 1 sign + 8 exponent (bias 127) + 23 fraction bits, worked example and the 0.1 != 0.1 warning.

🎡 The Number Playground — three interactive machines for this week: toggle 8 bits and watch the weights sum; spin the complement sundial (the same pattern read by four conventions — find the overflow cliff at 0111→1000, and the double zeros); and dissect IEEE FP32 live — flip an exponent bit and watch the value leap worlds.
Lec 3 — companion slides (Prof. Shweta Agrawal, IIT Madras)

title: W02: The Computer, Revisited · Number Systems
text:
PAGAL Notes
PAGAL — Perspectives on Algorithms, Generative AI & Learning: the week’s informal column.
How many bits does a number deserve? (FP32 → FP16 → NVFP4)
This week you met IEEE FP32 — the 32-bit costume the world agreed real numbers should wear: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 fraction bits, about seven trustworthy decimal digits. For thirty years that was simply what “a real number” meant in a computer. Then the AI industry asked a heretical question: who says a number deserves 32 bits?
The first cut was gentle. FP16 — “half precision” — keeps the same three-part anatomy but on a diet: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 fraction bits. Half the memory, twice the numbers per second through the same hardware, and for neural networks it mostly… worked. That “mostly” is the interesting part: a neural network is not a bank ledger. It is a huge fabric of approximate quantities whose collective pattern matters far more than any individual value’s seventh decimal digit. Precision, it turns out, was being spent where nobody was reading it — and this week’s deepest idea (meaning lives in the reader) applies to precision too.
So the diet continued: 8 bits, then four. NVIDIA’s current answer, introduced with its Blackwell chips, is NVFP4 (the official name — often misheard as “NFP4”). A single NVFP4 value is four bits in E2M1 anatomy: 1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 fraction bit. Stop and let that register against Deck 03: two exponent bits and one fraction bit can express only sixteen distinct values, with magnitudes no larger than ±6. As a stand-alone number format, that is almost comically poor — you could not price vegetables with it.
The rescue is a trick worth remembering, because it is pure Week-2 thinking. NVFP4 numbers never travel alone: they live in blocks of 16, and each block carries one shared scale factor — itself a small floating-point number (FP8, E4M3 anatomy) — with one full-precision FP32 scale over the whole tensor on top. Each little 4-bit value means “my sixteenth of the pattern, times my block’s scale, times the tensor’s scale.” The costume didn’t get smarter; the convention around it did — two levels of shared context squeeze meaning through a four-bit needle. It is positional notation’s own trick, one storey up: digits are cheap because the position carries the magnitude; here, values are cheap because the block carries it.
Why go through these contortions? Because at AI scale, bits are physics. A model with a trillion parameters stored in FP32 is four terabytes that must be fetched, again and again, through memory systems that burn energy per byte moved. Cut each number from 32 bits to 4 (plus a sliver for shared scales) and you have cut memory, bandwidth, and much of the energy bill by nearly 8× — which is the difference between an AI that runs in a datacenter and one that runs on your phone.
Three take-homes, all of them this course in miniature. Representation is a design choice, not a fact of nature — FP32 was never sacred, just convenient. The right representation depends on the reader — a bank reads every paisa; a neural network reads a pattern; giving both the same 32 bits wastes somebody’s silicon. And the frontier of computing in 2026 is being decided by exactly what you practised this week — exponents, fractions, biases, and the art of meaning more with fewer bits. The people designing whatever comes after NVFP4 are doing your Week 2 homework, for very high stakes.
Sources: NVIDIA Transformer Engine documentation on FP8/FP4 · NVFP4 format overview · NVFP4 vs MXFP4 decision guide.

A dose of curiosity: the five missing table entries that cost $475 million
In 1994, Thomas Nicely, a mathematics professor at a small college in Virginia, was doing something gloriously useless: computing Brun’s constant — the sum of the reciprocals of twin primes — to more digits than anyone had before. Pure curiosity; no product, no deadline. In June, he noticed his freshly assembled Pentium machine producing totals that disagreed, subtly, with his older machines and with published values.
Here is the part to study: he did not shrug. Almost anyone would have — blamed a library, a compiler, cosmic rays, themselves. Nicely spent months eliminating suspects one by one: his own code, the compiler, the operating system, the motherboard — until the only suspect left standing was the processor itself. In October 1994 he wrote to Intel; the young Internet did the rest.
The root cause is pure Week 2. The Pentium’s division hardware used a fast algorithm (SRT division) that looks up quotient digits in a table etched into the silicon — 1,066 entries. Five of them were missing — they read 0 where they should have read 2. Five wrong cells out of a thousand: divisions came out wrong only rarely, and when they did, the error typically appeared from about the fourth significant digit — the famous example being 4,195,835 ÷ 3,145,727, which the flawed chip got wrong where every ₹30 calculator got it right. Intel had noticed and quietly fixed new silicon; publicly it argued a typical user might hit the bug once in 9 billion divisions, and offered replacements only to users who could prove they needed accurate division. The Internet took that about as well as you’d expect. IBM halted Pentium shipments; in December Intel capitulated to a no-questions-asked recall — the first CPU recall in history — and wrote off $475 million.
Why does this belong in a week about number representation? Three reasons. First, representation is physical: your FP32 formula is not chalkboard decoration — it is implemented by actual transistors, and five absent ones silently corrupted arithmetic on millions of machines. Second, approximation errors do not stay where they are born: an error in the fourth digit of one division, fed into the next calculation and the next, compounds — in a long scientific computation, a spreadsheet of finances, or a structural simulation, a “tiny” representation error can explode into a wrong bridge load or a wrong drug dose. “It’s only the fourth digit” is not a sentence an engineer gets to say. And third — the temperament lesson this column keeps returning to — the bug was not found by Intel’s test suites. It was found by one curious person who checked his numbers against independent references and refused to shrug at a discrepancy in the ninth decimal place. The manufacturer had every resource; the professor had the audit habit. The habit won.
Thirty years later, a hobbyist put the actual flawed chip under a microscope and photographed the five missing cells in the silicon (Ken Shirriff’s analysis) — curiosity, again, closing the loop. Your 0.1 + 0.2 experiment this week is the same activity at student scale: don’t trust, don’t shrug, interrogate the representation.
Sources: Pentium FDIV bug — Wikipedia · Tom’s Hardware retrospective (30 years) · Ken Shirriff’s silicon-level analysis.

title: W03: Complements, Overflow · First C Program
text:
PAGAL Notes
PAGAL — Perspectives on Algorithms, Generative AI & Learning: the week’s informal column.
Three overflows: a rocket, a pop song, and a date in 2038
This week you computed 100 + 50 on eight bits and got −106 — a wrong answer delivered with total confidence, no alarm rung. It is worth knowing how far that little cliff scales.
June 4, 1996. The European Space Agency launches the first Ariane 5. Thirty-seven seconds later it tears itself apart. The inquiry traced it to one conversion: a 64-bit floating-point value — the rocket’s horizontal velocity — stuffed into a 16-bit signed integer, whose edge of the world is 32,767. The guidance software had been reused from Ariane 4, a slower rocket whose velocities always fit. Ariane 5 flew faster than its inherited representation imagined; the value overflowed; the guidance computers gave up; roughly half a billion dollars of rocket and satellites rained into a mangrove swamp. Notice what kind of mistake this is: not bad arithmetic — a GIVEN that silently changed while the spec stayed frozen. Week 1’s lesson, at orbital velocity: the spec is a model of the world, and the world had a new rocket in it.
December 2014. PSY’s “Gangnam Style” approaches 2,147,483,647 views — 2³¹ − 1, the +127 of the 32-bit world — and YouTube announces its view counter must move to 64 bits. The same number that ends your int ends a pop career’s counter. (YouTube, enjoying itself, made the counter spin when you hovered on it.)
January 19, 2038, 03:14:07 UTC. Unix systems that store time as seconds since 1970 in a signed 32-bit integer will hit the edge and wrap — to 1901. This is not retro trivia: embedded controllers, industrial systems, and careless new code written this year will still be running in 2038. Some of you will spend early-career months on exactly this — the way an earlier generation spent 1999 on Y2K.
The through-line, and the week’s moral: a representation is a promise about the future — “the values will always fit here.” Ariane’s promise was broken by a faster rocket, YouTube’s by an unexpected hit, Unix’s simply by time passing. When you choose int next week — and you will, hundreds of times — you are signing that promise. The engineers’ habit is to ask, every time: what happens at the edge, and who will be standing there when it arrives?
Sources: Ariane flight V88 — Wikipedia · UMN case archive: the Ariane 5 explosion · TechCrunch on the Gangnam Style counter · The Year 2038 problem — Epoch Converter.

title: W05: From Source to Executable
text:
PAGAL Notes
PAGAL — Perspectives on Algorithms, Generative AI & Learning: the week’s informal column.
The oldest version of “code you didn’t write”
This week you ran nm hello.o and found a single letter waiting for you: U printf. Undefined. Your program called a function you never wrote, never read, and — until Monday — never thought about. It compiled anyway. It ran anyway. It printed anyway.
Sit with how strange that is. Since Lab 01 you have been shipping programs whose behaviour depends on code you have not audited. Not a little of it: printf alone is thousands of lines of format-string parsing, buffering, and system calls. You trusted it completely, and you were right to — but notice that you never decided to trust it. The trust arrived pre-installed, in the shape of a #include line the lab sheet told you to type.
This is the oldest version of the problem everyone is arguing about in 2026. “Code you did not write, running in your program, doing things you have not verified” is not something AI invented. It is what a library is, and it is what the linker does for a living: take your unresolved promises and quietly bind them to somebody else’s implementation. The industry has been doing this since the 1950s. What has changed is not the nature of the problem but its scale and its provenance — the stranger’s code now arrives faster, in larger quantities, and from a source that cannot tell you where it came from.
So the interesting question is not “should I use code I didn’t write?” — you already do, hundreds of thousands of lines of it, every time you type gcc. The question is what makes trust reasonable. And the C library gives a genuinely good answer, worth naming because you will spend a career looking for it again: printf is trustworthy because it has a specification (the C standard says precisely what %d must do), because that specification is stable (code written in 1990 still works), and because it has been checked against that specification by more people, for longer, than almost any other artifact in engineering. Not because it is famous. Not because it usually works. Because someone wrote down what it must do, and then the world spent thirty-five years trying to catch it not doing that.
Measure the new stranger by the same ruler. When a machine hands you forty lines of C, ask the three questions the linker’s stranger can answer: what is it supposed to do, stated precisely enough to check? does that statement stay true tomorrow? and who has actually checked? Very often the honest answers are: nothing written down, no, and nobody. That is not a reason to refuse the code. It is a precise description of what you now have to supply — which is exactly the work this course keeps handing you, and exactly why your Lab 02 checker tested your program on numbers you had never seen.
There is a coda, and Monday earned it. Four programs stood between your source and your executable — preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker — and every one of them inspected your code with great rigour. Not one of them asked whether it solved the problem. The most sophisticated tooling in your possession is structurally incapable of the one check that matters most. That was true in 1975 and it is true of the newest model released this year: tools verify form; only you verify intent. The U was undefined until someone resolved it. So is the question of whether your program is right.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
section: One idea before you type anything
text:
One idea before you type anything
The terminal is the course’s third machine. It has a vocabulary of words; it runs the ritual you have already watched twice — read a command → execute it → print → repeat — and it does exactly what you say, never what you mean. Everything you learned from the Turtle applies. Everything.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
section: The map — read this aloud together before typing (5 min)
text:
The map — read this aloud together before typing (5 min)
Everything stored on this computer lives in one big tree. A folder (directory) is a box that can hold files and other boxes; a file is a page inside a box; a path is an address, read from the root / downward:
/                            ← the root: everything starts here
└── home
    └── student              ← the shared home
        └── csp_labs_f26
            └── w02-l01-…    ← YOUR workspace today
And the single most important fact of the day: you are always standing somewhere in this tree. Every command you type acts from where you stand. Three commands are your legs and eyes: pwd (where am I standing?), ls (what can I see from here?), and cd somewhere (walk there; cd .. walks one level up).






When the machine says No such file or directory it means: “from where I’m standing, I can’t see that name.” Do not panic, do not retype harder. Run the compass: 1) pwd — where am I? 2) ls — what’s actually here? 3) cd to the right place, then try again. Nine out of ten errors in this lab are cured by exactly this.









Copying commands. Only the command boxes on this page carry a copy button (top-right of the box) — everything else is for reading, not pasting. One box = one step: run a box, read what the machine said, then take the next box — never paste your way through three boxes blind. And careful: pasting into a terminal is not Ctrl+V — use Ctrl+Shift+V (and Ctrl+Shift+C to copy from the terminal). For short commands, though: type them. Fingers learn what eyes only skim.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
text:
Act 0 · Install (10 min)
The lab pack is pre-placed on each machine (ask where). If it isn’t — or you’re at home — fetch it from the course site:
wget https://acads-iit-jammu.github.io/csp-f26-dhavala/labs/lab01.tar.gz
Unpack it and run the installer:
tar xzf lab01.tar.gz
cd lab01
./install.sh
The installer will tell you which branch it thinks you are (it reads the machine’s name and today’s date — ask yourself: how?), ask for your team’s roll number(s), and build your session workspace: /home/student/csp_labs_f26/w02-l01-<branch>-sd. (Practising at home, where that path doesn’t exist? The installer switches to practice mode and creates the workspace right where you ran it — everything else works identically.) This machine is shared and forgets everything — your workspace lives for today only; your work leaves with you at the end (Act 5).
Now walk to your workspace. Do not type any * — your workspace’s exact name depends on your branch, and the installer just printed it for you under “Next steps”. Type the cd line it printed. It will look like this (yours may say ee, me or mt, and can end in -2 if another team used this machine first):
cd /home/student/csp_labs_f26/w02-l01-me-sd
Then the most important step of the day — start the session recorder. Everything you type and see from here on is recorded: your lab’s own machine diary. (To stop it later: type exit.)

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
text:
Act 1 · Claim the machine (10 min)
Who are you, where are you, on what? One box per question — predict the output before each Enter.
Who am I? (The answer is a surprise: you are all student — remember that for Act 5.)
whoami
Which machine is this?
hostname
What operating system, exactly?
uname -a
How much disk is free here?
df -h .
Now make the machine’s passport — your first redirection: > sends a command’s output into a file instead of the screen, and >> appends instead of overwriting. Writing the passport is one step (nothing appears on screen — that’s the point; it went into the file):
whoami > passport.txt
hostname >> passport.txt
uname -a >> passport.txt
df -h . >> passport.txt
Verifying it is the next step:
cat passport.txt

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
text:
Act 2 · Build the home (20 min)
Missions, each a mini spec-card: the ENSURES tells you what must be true when you’re done — you build it. Before every ls, say out loud what it will print — then press Enter.

Create a notes/ directory — your lab notebook. Two files will live in it: README.txt (one line saying what lives where in this workspace) and answers.txt, where you’ll write your answers to the think-questions this sheet asks along the way (they’re marked ✍️). Your notebook travels home in your bundle — we read it. ENSURES: cat notes/README.txt prints your line. (Tools: mkdir, nano.)
Build a practice/ tree, from nothing, yourself — you are the one creating every directory and file here. Target shape:
practice/
├── a/one.txt
├── a/two.txt
└── b/one.txt
Rules of the game: make the directories (mkdir -p practice/a practice/b), create the first file empty (touch), but the other two files may not be created by touch — one must be born as a copy (cp) and one must arrive by being moved (mv) from somewhere else you made. (So you’ll create a scratch file and move it — that’s the point.) ENSURES: ls -R practice matches the diagram exactly. Predict the output on paper first.
Now remove your practice/ tree — your first rm. Do it the careful way: rm -ri practice, and read every question it asks before answering. rm has no undo, no bin, no mercy. Respect it today, every day. ENSURES: ls no longer shows practice. (notes/ stays — it’s real; practice/ was scaffolding.)
Rescue skills — get stuck on purpose: open man ls, find what -a does, quit (press q). Try ls --help. Press Tab twice after typing pass. These three moves answer 90% of the questions you’d otherwise ask us.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
text:
Act 3 · Make it speak (15 min)
Your starter files are already in the workspace (the installer put them there). Open hello.c and put your name inside the quotes (both names, for pairs):
nano hello.c
Compile it (silence means success — the compiler only speaks when something is wrong):
gcc hello.c -o hello
Run it:
./hello
Run it again, capturing the output into a file this time (screen stays quiet — where did it go?):
./hello > output.txt
Count that file’s words by piping it through wc:
cat output.txt | wc -w
You just compiled a real C program — the same printf whose descent you watched, floor by floor, in Week 1. You’ll understand every line by Week 4; today it’s the telescope check.
✍️ Think-question 1, into notes/answers.txt: why the ./ in ./hello? Run echo $PATH and reason it out — ask us at the end if it doesn’t click.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
text:
Act 4 · Kill the runaway (10 min)
Week 2’s Toy Computer trapped itself in an infinite ping-pong and could only be Reset. Real machines give you a fire extinguisher. The starter loop.c is a program that never stops on purpose (it runs silently, so your terminal stays calm). Compile it:
gcc loop.c -o loop
Run it in the foreground and watch it not stop — then put it out with extinguisher #1: Ctrl-C:
./loop
Now start it in the background (that’s the &), where Ctrl-C cannot reach it:
./loop &
Find it. pgrep loop prints the runaway’s PID — its roll number, just the number:
pgrep loop
Kill that number — extinguisher #2 — replacing 12345 with the number your pgrep printed:
kill 12345
Confirm the fire is out — pgrep printing nothing means no such process remains:
pgrep loop
(Curious what pgrep is shorthand for? Run plain ps and find your loop in the crowd — that’s the long way, and on a shared machine it is a crowd.)






Remember this for later: ./loop &, pgrep, and kill <PID> are one-time commands. They must NOT go into your replay.sh in Act 6. That PID number was true for one moment on one machine; replayed later it could kill someone else’s process.



Every programmer writes an infinite loop eventually. Now you’ve already survived one.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
section: Act 5 · Lock up and take your work (15 min)
text:
Act 5 · Lock up and take your work (15 min)
Why permissions exist — thirty seconds of Unix’s soul. Your laptop or phone pretends to be yours alone. Unix never pretended: it was born in 1969 on machines that whole teams shared, and it is still built on that assumption — many people, one computer (exactly like this lab). So every file carries a small contract stating who may do what: three audiences — the file’s owner (u), the owner’s group (g), and others (o, everyone else) — times three rights — read, write, execute. That’s the rwxr-xr-x you see in ls -l: owner may read/write/execute; group may read/execute; others may read/execute. chmod (“change mode”) is how the owner rewrites that contract. Fifty years later, the same nine letters guard every server, every phone app’s sandbox, every cloud machine — because everything serious is shared.

Look at a permission string: ls -l hello. Decode rwxr-xr-x on paper: three groups of three bits — 111 101 101 = octal 755. This week’s number systems, wearing work clothes.
Try chmod 600 passport.txt, then ls -l passport.txt. ✍️ Think-question 2, into notes/answers.txt: you are all logged in as student — so who exactly did you just lock out? (Honest answer: nobody in this room. chmod guards between users, and this whole room is one user. That is what permissions really are — and why real systems give each person their own account.)
Stop the recorder (type exit — you’ll see “Script done”), then run the self-check:
./check.sh
Red lines tell you what’s missing, never how — that’s your job. bonus-open lines are not required today (they’re Act 6, at home). When the required lines are green — or when time is up; an imperfect bundle beats no bundle — bundle up:
./check.sh --bundle
The bundle (../lab01_<rolls>_<branch>_w02.tar.gz) is your work. Copy it out — Moodle upload (link announced in lab), and always also email yourself a copy. Then leave the machine clean: your workspace will be swept automatically before the next lab.

title: Lab 01: Move-In Day
section: Act 6 · Bonus, at home: your history becomes a program
text:
Act 6 · Bonus, at home: your history becomes a program
Do this on any machine — extract the lab pack anywhere and ./install.sh puts a practice workspace right where you run it.
Your recorded history is a log. Turn it into a program:
history > replay.sh
Open it and edit — rules below:
nano replay.sh






Editing rules — read before touching replay.sh:

Every line starts with a number (like 501  ./hello). Those are history bookkeeping, not commands — a replay would try to run a program called 501. Delete every line number.
Make the very first line exactly: #!/bin/sh — it tells the machine which language this program speaks.
KEEP only commands that make sense every time they run: ./hello, cat output.txt | wc -w, ls -l.
DELETE ./loop & — a replay would start a runaway with nobody watching.
DELETE pgrep and kill <PID> — that PID was true for one moment of one afternoon. Replay it tomorrow and you might kill a stranger’s process.
The self-check runs your replay.sh and reports it as a bonus item.




Now run it — before doing anything else:
./replay.sh
Permission denied! This is not an error — it is a lesson. A freshly created file is not allowed to run; you must grant it the execute permission yourself:
chmod +x replay.sh
Now it runs:
./replay.sh
✍️ Bonus for notes/answers.txt: in one line, what is the difference between a log and a program? (Hint: a log records what happened; a program must be true whenever it runs.) Anything you can do, you can automate — but only the repeatable parts.

text:
Act 2 · The graded five (50 min, solo)
Five files, e1.c … e5.c, already in your workspace. The spec is the comment at the top of each file — GIVEN, ENSURES, one public example. In brief:








Problem
Task
Final line ends with exactly




e1.c
sum & average of three integers (one scanf)

e2.c
circle area & circumference; π must be a named constant 3.14159; radius in a float

e3.c
quotient, remainder, decimal quotient

<H> h <M> m <S> s

How checking works — read this once, it’s the rules of the game:

./check.sh e1 compiles your source and runs it on test inputs; ./check.sh runs everything.
Public inputs (in each spec) you can test by hand. The checker also draws fresh random inputs from the GIVEN — its ranges are stated, nothing outside them is ever tested. So a program that merely memorizes the examples fails the next draw; only a program that computes survives. That is the point.
Your prompts are welcome — the checker only requires that the final line ends with the contract text.
Verdicts are honest: COMPILE-FAIL shows the compiler’s words; WRONG shows the input, your final line, and the expected line — play spot-the-difference.

Sixteen tiny programs. For each one you will see the code, write down what you think it prints, and only then run it.
./drill.sh --all
Predicting is the exercise. Running is only the marking. A wrong prediction is worth exactly as many marks as a right one — but only if you actually write it down first, so be honest with yourself. The one thing that earns nothing is running the program before you have committed to an answer.
What they cover:







Drills
Territory




d01–d04
integer vs. real division, % with negatives, where a cast goes


d05–d08
precedence, associativity, *=, chained assignment


d09–d12
characters as numbers, truncation, deriving the case gap


d13–d14
what printf rounds, pads, and refuses to add

./drill.sh on its own shows your progress. ./drill.sh 7 re-runs just number 7.






Drill 04 is the single most expensive misconception in this course. If you get it wrong, stop and stare at it until it is obvious — it comes back in f2, f5 and e2.

title: Lab 04: Loops
text:
What changes today
Lab pack: lab04.tar.gz — pre-placed on lab machines, downloadable for home practice.
Syllabus practical modules: 5 and 6 — for loops, and while / do-while loops. They are taught together on purpose: the three forms are one idea in three costumes, and converting between them is a better exercise than meeting them a week apart.

Act 2 · Fill the blanks (25 min)
Five programs, each missing its scanf and the lines that make the loop move.







File
What it does




b1_sum_while.c
add 1 + 2 + … + n, with a while


b2_sum_for.c
the same sum, as a for — convert it; do not copy it

Do b3 first, then feed your answer 0. It says zero digits — wrong, because a while checks before it runs, so the body never runs at all. b5 is the same problem with do-while, which checks after. That contrast is the entire reason C has three loops instead of one.

Problem

e2 has a public example worth reading twice: 900 → rev=9. Reversed, 900 is 009, and a number has no leading zeros. The checker will draw numbers ending in zero.
e3 is Euclid, 300 BC. The whole algorithm rests on one fact — gcd(a, b) is the same number as gcd(b, a % b). Check it by hand on 48 and 18 before you write anything. The pair keeps changing; the answer never does. That unchanging thing is a loop invariant, and it is why you may stop the moment b reaches 0.

Act 3 · The checked three (40 min, solo)








Problem
Task
Final line ends with exactly




e1.c
classify a triangle from three sides
type=equilateral | type=isosceles | type=scalene | type=invalid


e2.c
do a and b share a factor? the smallest one
a=<A> b=<B> common=<D> or a=<A> b=<B> coprime

the first multiple of 7 among five numbers

e1 — check validity first. Three lengths make a triangle only if every pair adds up to more than the third: 5 5 8 is a triangle, 2 3 9 is three sticks that will not meet. Then ask of your ladder: do my cases cover every possibility?
e2 — search upward from 2 and break the moment you find a number that divides both; the spec asks for the smallest, so there is no reason to look further. Two numbers sharing no factor above 1 are coprime — and you met their gcd in Lab 04. What is it? Predict what your program should print for 13 13 before you run it.
e3 — a loop that can end for two different reasons: you found one and broke out, or you ran out of numbers. After the loop your program still has to know which — that is what the two output lines demand. A search that keeps searching after it has found the answer reports the last hit, not the first.

text:
Interactive artifacts, handouts, and other student-facing files used in lectures and labs. Items are added here as the semester progresses, and are linked from the relevant weekly notes and lab sheets.








Item
What it is
Used in




📽️ Deck 01 — Logistics
Opening lecture slides: schedule, assessment, tools, and how the course works. (Slide deck — use arrow keys.)
Week 01


📽️ PAGAL: Programming in the Age of AI
The PAGAL column in slide form: the Specify–Verify loop, why programming is becoming a commodity, and Computational X — computation as every discipline’s second half.
Week 01


📽️ Deck 02 — What is a Computer?
Lecture 2 slides: computing vs computer vs programming vs computational thinking; the stored-program dividing line.
Week 01


🖨️ Hello, World — all the way down
printf, honestly: five instructions (read · write · move · count · check), a finger, and a code book. Act 1 prints “abba” in a two-letter world; Act 2 grows the book to ASCII and prints Hello, world! — same program, bigger data.
Week 01


📽️ Deck 03 — Number Systems
Week 02 slides: radix-q systems, binary↔︎decimal conversion, two’s complement, fixed point, and IEEE FP32 — ending at “how many bits does a number deserve?”
Week 02


🎡 The Number Playground
Three interactive machines: poke 8 bits and watch the decimal form; spin the complement sundial (one pattern, four reading conventions — find the overflow cliff and the double zeros); dissect a live IEEE FP32 bit by bit.
Week 02


📽️ Deck 04 — The Computer, Revisited
Recap of the Week-1 machines, the von Neumann architecture named, and the calculator-vs-computer dividing line: where does the procedure live?
Week 02


🧮 The Toy Computer
A complete von Neumann machine in 40 visible cells: program it in ten instructions, watch fetch–decode–execute narrated, and climb the six-rung ladder from sequencing to the recursion wall.
Week 02


🔧 Under the Hood — Part 1: The Parts
The guided climb, stations 0–3: a switch flipped by a wire (the logical transistor), gates discovered by wiring switches in series and parallel, and a real ripple adder — arithmetic is wiring.
Week 02


🔧 Under the Hood — Part 2: Memory & Time
Stations 4–5: feed a gate its own output and it remembers (build a flip-flop from two NOR gates), then the clock — set the bell’s rhythm too fast and watch the notebook faithfully record garbage.
Week 02


🔧 Under the Hood — Part 3: The Machine
Stations 6–7: a machine built entirely from your own parts — registers of flip-flops, a control unit that is itself two flip-flops, a hand-cranked clock and live timing diagram — then the ladder back up to c = a + b;.
Week 02


📦 lab01.tar.gz
The Lab 01 pack: installer (infers your branch from the machine), starters, and the self-check. Extract, ./install.sh, follow the lab sheet.
Lab 01


📽️ Deck 07 — Types, Assignments & Operators
W03 Tuesday: the type wardrobe (size + reading convention), = as “gets”, operator precedence & associativity, promotion/truncation/casts, and six predict-the-output traps.
Week 03


📽️ Deck 05 — Complements & Overflow
W03 Monday: one’s & two’s complement fully worked, arithmetic with them, and overflow — the silent cliff, from 8-bit examples to Ariane 5.
Week 03


📽️ Deck 06 — Your First C Program
W03 Tuesday: hello.c line by line; gcc and ./ annotated word by word; variables as named cells with a reading convention; the integer-division surprise.
Week 03


📽️ Deck 10 — One Session at a Bank
W06: every control-flow construct arriving because an ATM session demanded it — for for a known count of attempts, while for a session of unknown length, switch for five discrete commands, continue for a refused transaction, and the quit bug that proves break leaves only the nearest construct. Design, not code.
Week 06


📽️ Deck 09 — Why Assemblers and Linkers Exist
The companion to Deck 08: not what the four stages do but why anyone built it that way — separate compilation, deliberately incomplete object files, relocation made visible with objdump -r, and the principle underneath: delay a decision until it reaches the component that can make it.
Week 05


🖨️ Floor and Ceiling — one problem, two loops
The loops handout: why casting to int is not floor, bracket-then-bisect, the invariant L < X < U as the correctness argument, a measured cost table (×1000 input → +20 steps), and two ways the program can lie — signed overflow into an infinite loop, and 2⁵³.
Week 05


🖨️ Why Assemblers and Linkers Exist — notes
The same material as a printable handout, with the two-minute add() experiment written out: gcc -c succeeds, linking fails, and the difference tells you what each tool is actually asking.
Week 05


📦 w05-practice.tar.gz
The Week 05 practice pack: 25 predict-then-run items — 14 precedence drills and the 11-step walk through the compiler pipeline (preprocessor → compiler → assembler → linker), each with the lesson it teaches. tar xzf, then ./practice.sh --all.
Week 05


📽️ Deck 08 — From Source to Executable
W05 Monday: Lab 03’s checked three worked through, then the compilation pipeline — preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker — each stage stopped and inspected, ending at nm and the U printf that explains why linkers exist.
Week 05


🐢 The Turtle Computer
Your first programming language: ten words, one turtle, no typing. Six missions in which each new word is invented because a problem demands it — and the reward comes only when the machine’s output matches your intention.
